opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few things that need to improve at the same time. The first is reasoning and planning. Today, models are quite good at answering a single question, but when you ask them to chain ten or twenty steps together, errors compound. If each step is 95% reliable, after twenty steps you're not reliable at all. So we need models that can plan better, notice when they've made a mistake, and backtrack. That's partly a training question, and partly about letting models spend more compute at inference time to think before they act.

The second is function calling and tool use. An agent is only as useful as the systems it can interact with, so models need to be very precise about calling APIs, reading the outputs, and deciding what to do next. That sounds mundane, but it's where a lot of failures happen in practice.

The third is evaluation, which I think is underrated. It's hard to improve agents if you can't measure whether they're doing the task correctly. In enterprises, every workflow is a bit different, so you need ways to define what success looks like for a specific use case, collect feedback, and feed it back into the system. That loop of deploying, measuring, and improving is where a lot of the value will come from.

And finally there's latency and cost. Agents make many calls to the model, so if each call is slow or expensive, the whole thing becomes impractical. That's why we care so much about efficient models. Smaller, faster models that are good enough for most steps, combined with larger models when you really need them, make agentic systems economically viable.

So it's not a single breakthrough. It's better reasoning, better tool use, better evaluation, and more efficiency, all coming together.

r001.rationale: It says smaller, faster models can make agentic systems economically viable.

r002.rationale: It does not identify repetitive agent loops as mode collapse.

r003.rationale: It mentions spending more inference compute and using larger models when needed, but does not clearly say to adapt computation to task difficulty.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think there are a few things, and they're not all about the model.

The first one is obviously reasoning, and in particular reasoning over long horizons. Today if you ask a model to do a task that takes two steps, it works. If you ask it to do a task that takes fifty steps, with tool calls and intermediate results, the error compounds and at some point it drifts. So a big part of it is training the model to plan, to verify its own intermediate outputs, to recover when something fails rather than hallucinating that it succeeded. That's mostly a training problem, it's reinforcement learning on actual environments, and I think we're still early on how to build those environments at scale.

The second thing is memory and context. Agents need to operate on the state of the world, and the state of the world is large. Longer context helps, but it's not enough. You need the model to be able to retrieve, to compress what it has seen, and to know what matters. That's partly architecture, partly how you set up the system around the model.

The third one, and I think people underestimate it, is latency and cost. An agent is making many calls. If each call takes ten seconds and costs a lot, the whole thing is impractical, and you can't do the kind of search, sampling, self-verification that actually makes agents reliable. So efficiency, small models that are good at specific steps, fast inference, this is what makes agentic systems economically viable. That's a big part of why we care about open models you can run close to your data.

And then the last thing is less technological and more about interfaces. Agents need to connect to tools, to software, to enterprise systems. Those systems were built for humans. So there's a lot of work on standardizing how a model talks to a tool, how you give it permissions, how you observe what it did. Without that, even a very capable model is stuck.

So I'd say: better long-horizon reasoning through RL, better memory, much cheaper and faster inference, and standardized tool interfaces. Put those together and agents stop being demos and start being deployed.

r001.rationale: The response recommends using “small models” for specific steps and connects efficiency and lower cost to making agent systems economically viable.

r002.rationale: It does not identify repetitive agent loops as mode collapse.

r003.rationale: It does not propose varying computation according to task difficulty.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a few things. One is making models better at planning over longer horizons. Today, a model can take a useful action, but if you ask it to carry out a sequence of twenty or thirty actions, errors accumulate. You need models that can recognize when something has gone wrong, revise their plan, and recover.

Another is the ability to learn from feedback from the environment. If an agent writes code, it can run it and look at the result. That gives it a way to check its work. Extending that kind of feedback to other tasks is going to be very useful.

And then there’s efficiency. Agents make many model calls, so latency and cost become much more significant than in a chatbot. You want to use a small, fast model for straightforward actions and spend more computation when the task actually requires reasoning. I think progress on those three fronts would make agents substantially more useful.

r001.rationale: The response connects agent efficiency to cost and proposes using a small, fast model for straightforward actions.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify repetitive loops as a form of mode collapse.

r003.rationale: It proposes spending more computation when a task requires reasoning and using a small, fast model for straightforward actions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a few things. One is getting models to reason over longer horizons—to make a plan, execute a step, look at the result, and revise the plan when something goes wrong. Being good at answering a question is different from being reliable over a sequence of actions.

Another is improving how models interact with tools and get feedback from the environment. If an agent writes code, it should be able to run it, inspect the errors, and correct itself. You want to train that entire loop, rather than just the production of an answer.

Memory is also important: keeping the relevant information as a task progresses without having to put everything back into the context. And all of this needs to be fast and inexpensive enough that you can afford multiple attempts. I think the progress will come from better models and from better systems around those models.

r001.rationale: It says agents need to be fast and inexpensive, but does not identify reducing model size as a way to achieve that.

r002.rationale: It describes revising plans and training tool-use loops, but does not identify repetitive loops as mode collapse.

r003.rationale: It mentions affordability and multiple attempts, but does not propose adapting computation to task difficulty.
